A2.text:
Kamran works in a big bank in Baku. He is a very serious person. He only reads non-fiction. He likes books about real history and facts.

His friend Lala loves fiction. One day, they are drinking tea in a small cafe on Nizami Street. Lala takes a digital device from her black bag.

“I have a new e-book for you,” Lala says. “It is about a famous old robbery in Sheki. It is very exciting.”

Kamran takes it. “Who is the author?” he asks.

“Just read the first chapter,” she answers with a smile.

That evening, Kamran sits in his quiet living room. He looks at his tall bookshelf. It is full of boring history books. He opens the new e-book.

The story is amazing. The bank robbers are very clever. Kamran reads all night. He does not sleep. He reads every word and finishes the whole book.

The next morning, he meets Lala near the bank. He is very excited.

“That non-fiction book was incredible!” Kamran says. “The old robbery in Sheki was so interesting. I want to go there and search for the real money.”

Lala laughs loudly. “Kamran, there is no real money. It is a fiction book!”

Kamran is shocked. “But it felt so real! Who wrote it?”

Lala smiles. “I did. It is my very first novel.”

B1.text:
Kamran was a senior manager at a large bank in Baku, and he did everything strictly by the book. In his free time, he only read non-fiction. He preferred reading about real historical events, biographies, or business facts, completely ignoring stories that were not true.

His friend Lala was the exact opposite. She loved fiction and always tried to share her favourite novels with him. One Friday evening, while they were having tea at a busy cafe near the Boulevard, Lala placed a digital e-reader on the table.

“I downloaded a new e-book for you,” she said. “It is a thrilling historical narrative about a famous bank robbery in Sheki during the nineteenth century.”

Kamran picked it up with a frown. “Who is the author?”

“Don’t worry about the author yet,” Lala smiled. “Just promise me you will try the first chapter.”

Later that night, Kamran sat on his comfortable sofa. He planned to read just ten pages, but the story was a genuine page-turner. The details of the old cobblestone streets and the clever robbers were absolutely fascinating. For the first time in his life, Kamran managed to completely lose himself in a book. He stayed awake until three in the morning just to find out how the daring robbery ended.

The next day, he called Lala immediately. “That non-fiction book was brilliant!” he told her. “The robbery was planned so perfectly. I actually want to travel to Sheki this weekend to see the old bank building.”

Lala started laughing on the phone. “Kamran, there is no old bank building. The whole story is fiction!”

Kamran was silent for a moment. “But the details were so incredibly realistic! Who wrote it?”

“I did,” Lala replied proudly. “I finally finished my first novel, and you were my very first reader!”

B2.text:
Kamran, a senior compliance officer at a major bank in Baku, lived his entire life strictly by the book. His modern apartment was always spotless, his daily routines were extremely rigid, and he exclusively read non-fiction. To Kamran, literature was only valuable if it delivered concrete facts; he considered imaginary stories a complete waste of time.

His childhood friend Lala, on the other hand, was an open book. She was highly expressive, delightfully disorganised, and passionately obsessed with fiction. One rainy Friday evening, while they were sharing a pot of thyme tea at a cozy cafe in Icherisheher, Lala slid her digital e-reader across the dark wooden table.

“I’ve loaded a new e-book for you,” she announced. “It’s a gripping historical narrative detailing a legendary, unsolved bank heist in Sheki back in 1895.”

Kamran adjusted his glasses and inspected the screen. “Who is the exact author? I don’t recognise the name on the cover.”

“Don't overthink it,” Lala said with a mischievous grin. “Just get through the first chapter. If you hate it, you can return to your boring biographies.”

That evening, Kamran stood before his massive bookshelf, bypassing his heavy volumes on economics to pick up the small digital device. He sat in his leather armchair, intending to skim a few pages before sleep. However, the manuscript was an absolute page-turner. The vivid descriptions of the misty Sheki mountains and the intricate mechanics of the bank vault were masterfully detailed. For the first time in a decade, Kamran allowed himself to completely lose himself in a book. He read continuously until dawn, desperate to uncover the clever robbers’ fate.

He phoned Lala the moment his morning alarm rang. “That non-fiction account was an absolute masterpiece!” he exclaimed. “The logistical planning of the heist was flawless. I’m seriously thinking about driving to Sheki this weekend to locate the ruins of that specific bank.”

Lala’s loud laughter echoed through the phone receiver. “Kamran, there is no ruined bank. The entire story is pure fiction!”

Kamran was stunned into silence. “That’s impossible. The historical accuracy was astonishing. Who actually wrote it?”

“I did,” Lala beamed happily. “It’s my debut novel, and I’ve just proved that even you can enjoy a made-up story.”

questions.why: “The vivid descriptions of the misty Sheki mountains and the intricate mechanics of the bank vault were masterfully detailed” and he later mentions “historical accuracy”.

questions.why: An “open book” is an idiom for someone whose thoughts and feelings are easy to read and obvious.

options: Because he had promised Lala he would try reading the first chapter of her e-book
He had already read all of them
He wanted to sell them to buy more fiction
They were too dusty to hold
questions.why: Lala had asked him to “just get through the first chapter,” so he bypassed his usual books to pick up the digital device.

podcast.title: Three in the morning

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you read more paper books or e-books? Guess: why does Leyla look so tired today?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is books and reading. And Leyla looks very tired today.
[laugh] I am! I started a novel on Sunday evening, and I couldn't stop. I finished the last chapter at three in the morning.
Ah, a real page-turner. What's it about?
It's a mystery. A woman finds an old letter inside a library book, and she tries to find the person who wrote it. The narrative jumps between today and the 1950s.
That sounds great. Who's the author?
A young Turkish writer — it's her first novel. Honestly, that's my favourite feeling: to lose yourself in a book and forget about time.
I'm the opposite. I almost never read fiction. I like non-fiction — history, science, the lives of real people.
And do you read paper books?
Mostly e-books, on my phone, on the metro. I can carry two hundred books in my pocket.
Practical. But I love paper. My grandfather had a huge bookshelf in his living room, from the floor to the ceiling.
Did he let you read everything?
Everything! He read every evening with a glass of tea, and I sat on the carpet next to him with my own little book.
I love that. My dad was different. He did everything by the book — even reading. He finished every book he started, even the boring ones.
[laugh] I don't do that. If a book is boring after fifty pages, I stop.
Me too. Life is too short. So what makes a book good for you?
The characters. I like a hero who is an open book — no secrets, every feeling right there on the page. And then a surprise at the end.
For me, it's what I learn. After a good history book, I see the world a little differently.
Maybe we should start a SpeakLab book club. One short book a month, and we talk about it on a call.
Great idea. But please, no books that keep me awake until three.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is the best book you have ever read — and why should your partner read it?
Mine is a history book about old ships. See you next time!
Bye for now!
